Subject: Private deployment — network options and constraints

Hi Naomi,

Thanks for the chat this morning. To recap our environment and what we need from Redwood Private: we plan to host the inference cluster in our AWS account (us-east-1), data must remain in US-only regions, and we expect sustained bursts of ~15k inference requests/min with 99.9% availability requirement during business hours.

Two items we need help with before procurement:
- Recommendation on connectivity pattern: VPC peering (cross-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or site-to-site VPN (managed VPN from our on-prem). Please include security and operational tradeoffs.
- Ballpark cost and how each option impacts SLA (failover, MTTR, and redundancy).

Attached a simple network diagram and our current traffic profile. We have a security review next Thursday and would like your recommendation + risks by Tuesday.

Brief answers are fine — we mainly need a clear recommendation and next steps for a PoC.

Sara

Sara — thanks for the clear summary and the diagram. High level recommendations below (I'll follow up with more detail and an XLS comparing cost and SLA implications). Attached: quick draft SLA/cost worksheet and an updated network diagram with labels.

Quick summary (short answer):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) — recommended for MedSys if you want strong service isolation, per-endpoint access control, and simplified routing. Pros: not transitive, less blast radius across accounts, supports explicit ALB/NLB->ENI patterns and integrated with VPC endpoints policies. Cons: slightly higher egress costs and may require more endpoint interfaces across AZs.

- VPC peering (cross-account) — pros: lower per-GB cost, simpler for high-throughput east-west traffic within a single region. Cons: no transitive routing (if you need central transit, it gets messy), route table sprawl, and cross-account peering requires careful IAM and network policy coordination. Peering complicates multi-account security boundaries and auditing.

- Site-to-site VPN (managed IPsec to on-prem) — best when you need encrypted tunnel to on-prem resources or have existing network appliances. Pros: straightforward for hybrid on-prem access. Cons: higher latency, limited throughput per tunnel (requires multiple tunnels and BGP for failover), and less predictable MTTR for cloud-to-cloud failover compared to PrivateLink.

SLA/operational notes: PrivateLink gives us the easiest way to provide controlled, per-consumer connectivity with deterministic failover strategies (multi-AZ endpoints + health checks). Peering can meet your throughput needs but will push more operational burden onto MedSys for route management and cross-account security. VPN is fine for initial PoC if you need on-prem proof, but it won't scale elegantly for the production SLOs you listed.

Next steps:
1) Karthik will own a ballpark cost delta (PrivateLink vs Peering) and put numbers in the attached spreadsheet.
2) Marissa can draft a short technical appendix with MTU/routing/HA considerations and a suggested PoC plan (2-week PoC: PrivateLink in us-east-1 with cross-AZ endpoints).
3) We'll prepare a short security matrix for your review by Tue.

If you want, we can tentatively schedule a 30-min technical deep-dive on Mon.

—Naomi

FYI — forwarding Sara's request and Naomi's summary. I'll pull numbers for cost per TB and estimated endpoint counts. Preliminary notes for consideration:

- Cost model to compare: PrivateLink charges per-hour per endpoint ENI + data processing per GB; peering charges generally only inter-AZ data transfer (lower), VPN has per-hour tunnel costs plus data egress. We should present a 12-month TCO with a mid and high-traffic scenario.
- Operational overhead: peering => more route table entries and potential need for centralized transit (Transit Gateway) if they grow to multiple VPCs/accounts. If MedSys intends to connect multiple consumer VPCs to our service, PrivateLink can reduce blast radius but increase endpoint count.
- Compliance: PrivateLink maps cleanly to our recommendation for strict logging and private connectivity — it fits SOC2 narratives better in many cases.

I'll draft numbers and attach to Naomi's sheet. Marissa, can you confirm any model constraints we should call out (e.g., maximum interface endpoints per ENI, AZ replication, transient throttling)?

-Karthik

On Sun, Jul 20, 2025 at 08:15, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai> wrote:
> FYI — forwarding Sara's request and Naomi's summary. I'll pull numbers for cost per TB and estimated endpoint counts. Preliminary notes for consideration:

Adding a few operational/technical tradeoffs from the infra side:

1) MTU and fragmentation: VPN tunnels often have reduced MTU; for high-throughput inference traffic this can add overhead and increase CPU on appliances if fragmentation occurs. PrivateLink and peering preserve VPC-level MTU (subject to ENI limits), so they tend to be more efficient for token-level streaming workloads.

2) Failover and HA: For PrivateLink, create interface endpoints in at least 2 AZs and put NLB in front of the Redwood Private service in each AZ. Health checks enable failover without touching peering route tables. For peering, you must coordinate active/passive routing or use Transit Gateway for simpler multi-VPC architectures.

3) Cross-account IAM and auditing: Peering requires more explicit cross-account routing and NACL adjustments; PrivateLink lets you scope by endpoint policy and VPC endpoint service permissions, which simplifies least-privilege enforcement.

4) Diagnostics and observability: With PrivateLink we can instrument private endpoints and provide per-VPC telemetry more easily. Peering traffic is harder to attribute to a particular consumer without VPC Flow Logs analysis and label conventions.

Suggested PoC configuration (2 weeks):
- Build PrivateLink service in our us-east-1 account with NLB backed by Redwood Private instances (2 AZs).
- Create endpoint in MedSys's primary VPC (they open Selective endpoint policy and subnets).
- Run synthetic throughput tests (see attached privatelink-latency-test.txt) and compare to a short peering test (single AZ peering) to show delta.

I'll also note resource limits: AWS has default quotas on interface endpoints per region/account; we'll include quota requests in the PoC plan if needed.

-Marissa

Thanks Naomi, Karthik, Marissa — this is exactly what we needed.

We reviewed the tradeoffs with security and architecture leads here. Given our compliance needs and the desire to minimize cross-account blast radius, we're inclined to move forward with the PrivateLink first for the PoC. Actions we want from Redwood:
1) A short cost delta (PrivateLink vs peering) for the two traffic profiles — please include 12-month projection and call out endpoint counts by AZ.
2) PoC runbook (steps below) and a request for any quota increases we should submit to AWS.
3) SLA note: would Redwood be willing to include an addendum that documents expected MTTR for endpoint/NLB failures and a remediation playbook for cross-AZ failover? We may require this to satisfy our procurement.

PoC runbook (what we expect):
- Create PrivateLink service + NLBs (Redwood) in us-east-1 across 2 AZs.
- Create endpoint in our VPC and verify connectivity to a sandbox model instance.
- Run synthetic stream test (15k req/min baseline + 50% spike) for 48 hours.
- Share logs/metrics and a short postmortem.

If you can get the cost delta and PoC runbook to us by Tue EOD we'll route it to procurement and security.

Sara
